decisions.title: Annual Plan 2026/27 adopted — 7.9% average rates rise
decisions.outcome: The Governing Body adopted the Annual Plan 2026/2027, confirming a 7.9% average residential rates rise (about $321/year for an average household) after a last-minute councillor amendment to cut it to 5.9% failed. decisions.title: Council takes back day-to-day transport control from 1 October
decisions.outcome: Following the Transport Governance Amendment Act 2026, Council endorsed a "Quick Fixes" work programme so it — rather than Auckland Transport — will directly resolve everyday issues like blocked lanes and confusing road markings from 1 October 2026, ahead of the full transport-governance handover.

decisions.title: Congestion (time-of-use) charging options endorsed
decisions.outcome: The Transport, Infrastructure and Delivery Committee endorsed three congestion-charging zone options — city centre, city fringe, and key motorway locations, at an estimated $2–$7 per trip — and an engagement approach, moving Auckland toward its first congestion charge.

decisions.title: 30-year transport spending roadmap approved
decisions.outcome: The Transport, Infrastructure and Delivery Committee approved a 30-year transport investment policy statement setting principles for future spending, ahead of the full Regional Land Transport Plan.

upcoming.title: Congestion charging public consultation
upcoming.detail: Public engagement on the three endorsed time-of-use charging options is expected to open around November 2026, ahead of a future council decision on which option, if any, to adopt.

upcoming.title: Full transport-governance handover completes
upcoming.detail: The new Auckland Regional Transport Committee and the shift of most transport functions from Auckland Transport to Council are due to be fully operational by November 2026, six months after the Transport Governance Amendment Act 2026 came into force.

keyIssues.text: Council adopted a 7.9% average rates rise for 2026/27 after navigating a $213 million budget risk (which could have forced a 15% rise) and finding $106 million in savings. Affordability of rates versus service and infrastructure funding remains contested — a last-minute amendment to cut the rise to 5.9% narrowly failed.

keyIssues.title: Transport governance reform & congestion charging
keyIssues.text: The Transport Governance Amendment Act 2026 is shifting most road-control functions from Auckland Transport back to Council, via a new joint Auckland Regional Transport Committee. In parallel, Council is advancing Auckland's first congestion (time-of-use) charge, with options priced at roughly $2–$7 per trip.

keyIssues.title: City Rail Link & network transformation
keyIssues.text: The City Rail Link — a 3.45km twin-tunnel underground rail link with three new stations (Te Waihorotiu, Karanga-a-Hape, Maungawhau) — opens 13 September 2026, bringing a new timetable and much higher service frequency. It is the single largest cost driver behind recent rates decisions.

keyIssues.title: Water services reform (Local Water Done Well)
keyIssues.text: Auckland's water services sit under the Government's Local Water Done Well programme, with Watercare operating as a more financially independent council-controlled organisation. Governance costs remain contentious — councillors rejected a 33% fee-rise proposal for CCO directors, including Watercare's board, as unaffordable.

keyIssues.title: Flooding resilience — Making Space for Water
keyIssues.text: Council's Making Space for Water programme continues rolling out flood-resilience projects across flood-prone areas such as Māngere/Harania, following the 2023 Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle. A May 2026 Auditor-General's office review praised the programme for delivering flood protection efficiently and at good value.

mayor.name: Moko Tepania
mayor.note: Independent — re-elected Mayor in October 2025 with 10,502 votes, defeating Ann Court (3,259 votes). Of Te Rarawa and Ngāti Kahu ki Whangaroa descent, a te reo Māori teacher based in Kaikohe, first elected councillor in 2019 and became Northland's youngest-ever and the Far North's first Māori mayor in 2022. Rated NZ's most popular mayor in a March 2026 Taxpayers' Union–Curia poll. This term's priorities include roading and water infrastructure contracts, driving a proposed new Northland-wide local government structure, and rates affordability. Announced in November 2025 he will not seek re-election in 2028.

decisions.outcome: Council signed off on joining Northland Waters (Ngā Wai o Te Tai Tokerau) with Whangārei and Kaipara district councils, which will take over council water and wastewater infrastructure and debt from July 2027.

upcoming.title: Government decision on Northland local government reform
upcoming.detail: Ministers are expected to decide whether the Northland unitary-authority proposal proceeds; if approved, public consultation would run from October 2026 with a detailed proposal due by March 2027.

upcoming.detail: A councillor motion requiring a formal significance assessment and public engagement before six proposed iwi relationship agreements are signed was before council.

keyIssues.title: Rates affordability
keyIssues.text: Far North has some of the highest rates burdens relative to income in New Zealand. The 2026/27 rise was held to 6.7% only via roughly $5m in Far North Holdings dividends plus budget savings, after a higher figure was originally signalled.

keyIssues.title: Roading & infrastructure resilience
keyIssues.text: Ongoing tendering of roading contracts and infrastructure repair are a top mayoral priority, reflecting the district's large, sparsely populated, storm- and flood-prone road network.

keyIssues.title: Water services reform (Local Water Done Well)
keyIssues.text: Far North is transferring its water and wastewater assets and debt into a new joint Northland water entity, Northland Waters, from July 2027 — a major structural and financial change for ratepayers.

keyIssues.title: Local government amalgamation
keyIssues.text: A live, high-stakes process: Far North, Whangārei and Northland Regional Council back a staged unitary-authority model, while Kaipara opposes it — creating regional tension ahead of a government decision expected around September 2026.

keyIssues.title: Māori ward representation
keyIssues.text: A binding local poll held alongside the October 2025 election on retaining the Ngā Tai o Tokerau Māori ward passed (10,980 to keep vs 9,292 to remove), settling the question through the 2028 and 2031 elections.

decisions.title: Council backed the Northland "Head Start" reform outline
decisions.outcome: Council unanimously supported a proposal for Whangārei and Kaipara to initially merge into one unitary authority, with Far North separate and a shared regional body from 2028; submitted to central government by the 9 August 2026 deadline.

upcoming.title: Northland reform public consultation
upcoming.detail: If the Head Start proposal is accepted by central government, detailed analysis and public consultation on a Whangārei–Kaipara unitary authority model is expected to begin.

upcoming.title: Chief Executive recruitment
upcoming.detail: Chief Executive Simon Weston departs after 30 years' service; council must decide interim leadership arrangements and run a recruitment process for his replacement.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform / possible unitary authority
keyIssues.text: Central government's "Head Start" process could see Whangārei and Kaipara merge into one unitary council, with a single Northland-wide authority as the eventual goal. Kaipara has resisted this model, creating regional tension over the district's future shape.

keyIssues.title: Rates affordability and infrastructure funding
keyIssues.text: After a 2025/26 rate hike that drew hundreds of submissions, mostly from pensioners, the district settled on a 5% rise for 2026/27 — but total bills are rising faster once new water charges are folded in, keeping affordability a live political issue.

keyIssues.title: Three Waters / Local Water Done Well
keyIssues.text: Whangārei is moving its drinking water and wastewater into a new joint Northland-wide CCO, Northland Waters, with Kaipara and Far North, operational from July 2027 — a major structural and cost change for ratepayers.

keyIssues.title: Council–hapū relations
keyIssues.text: The June 2026 vote against a Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreement, alongside central government's move to scrap such statutory arrangements nationally, has strained relations with Ngā Hapū o Whangārei and raised questions about future engagement with tangata whenua.

keyIssues.title: Housing growth and roading capacity
keyIssues.text: Council-backed roading works have been positioned as unlocking land for thousands of new homes in northern Whangārei, keeping growth-related infrastructure a persistent council focus.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform / possible amalgamation
keyIssues.text: Central government's local-government reform agenda has put Northland's three councils at odds over whether to merge into two or three unitary authorities, with Kaipara publicly opposing the model backed by Whangārei and Far North.

keyIssues.title: Water services delivery (Local Water Done Well)
keyIssues.text: Kaipara is moving drinking water and wastewater delivery into a new shared entity, Northland Waters Limited, ahead of a July 2027 go-live — a major structural and cost change for ratepayers.

keyIssues.title: Rates affordability

keyIssues.title: District Plan review
keyIssues.text: A lengthy, high-volume hearings process covering 365+ submissions is reshaping land-use rules district-wide, from sites of significance to Māori through to general development provisions.

keyIssues.title: Roading
keyIssues.text: Ongoing state highway and local road funding and recovery work — including storm and flood road-recovery projects — is a persistent theme in council decision-making.
